newsitem.title: USA: Study backs go-slow approach for prostate cancer.
newsitem.headline: Study backs go-slow approach for prostate cancer.

text.p: A Swedish study published on Tuesday said survival rates for men with localised prostate cancer seem to be the same for those who simply wait to see what develops as for those who opt for surgery.

But the American Urological Association called the finding limited, saying it still believes younger men and those with at least a decade of life expectancy should be aggressively treated when diagnosed with the cancer.

The Swedish study was based on 300 prostate cancer patients whose disease had not spread beyond the gland and who were followed over a 15-year period. At the end of that time the survival rate was 81 percent among 233 of the men who received deferred treatment and 81 percent among those who received initial radical treatment.

"Patients with localised prostate cancer have a favourable outlook following watchful waiting, and the number of deaths potentially avoidable by radical initial treatment is limited," said the study from Orebro Medical Centre and Uppsala University.
"Without reliable prognostic indicators, an aggressive approach to all patients with early disease would entail substantial overtreatment," the study said.
The report was published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association.

An editorial in the same issue cautioned that the Swedish results may be deceiving because the men involved in that research had a mean age of 72 with tumours that were smaller and better differentiated.

The editorial said there is a growing concensus that the "watchful waiting" approach may be ideal for men who are too old or too ill to live another 15 years, for men without symptoms in whom the tumour is too far advanced to cure and in some men with small, well-defined tumours who elect for observation rather than surgery.

The Urological Association in a separate statement said the Swedish study presents only a "limited snapshot" while a comprehensive review of medical literature indicates the course of treatment should hinge on age and life expectancy.
